content: The concept of intentionality is often described as aboutness, referring to the relationship between mental acts and the external world. Historically, intentionality originated in scholastic philosophy and was later reintroduced into 19th-century contemporary philosophy by Franz Brentano in his work Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint (1874). Brentano defined intentionality as a distinguishing feature of mental phenomena, setting them apart from physical phenomena (physische Phänomene). He used terms such as reference to a content, direction toward an object, or immanent objectivity to describe this characteristic. According to Brentano, every mental phenomenon, or psychological act, has a content and is directed at an object, which he called the intentional object. This includes beliefs, desires, and other mental states. Brentano also introduced the term intentional inexistence to describe the status of the objects of thought within the mind. The presence of intentionality, or the directedness toward an intentional object, was the key feature that distinguished mental phenomena from physical phenomena, as physical phenomena lack intentionality entirely. The concept of intentionality gained broader attention in modern philosophy through the works of Edmund Husserl, who adopted and expanded upon Brentano's ideas. French philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre, in Being and Nothingness, equated intentionality with consciousness, arguing that the two are indistinguishable. This view contrasted sharply with Brentano's position, which regarded intentionality as merely one quality of mental phenomena. German philosopher Martin Heidegger, in Being and Time, redefined intentionality as care (Sorge), a condition that reflects an individual's existentiality, facticity, and engagement with the world, emphasizing its ontological significance as opposed to mere thinghood (ontic). In the 20th century, philosophers such as Gilbert Ryle and A.J. Ayer criticized Husserl's layered concept of consciousness and intentionality. Ryle argued that perceiving is not a process, while Ayer contended that describing knowledge does not involve describing mental processes. These critiques led to the view that consciousness is so inherently intentional that mental acts are emptied of all content, aligning with Sartre's notion of consciousness as nothing. Roderick Chisholm revived Brentano's thesis through linguistic analysis, distinguishing between the ontological and psychological aspects of intentionality. Chisholm's work sought to clarify the criteria for intentionality, identifying logical properties that differentiate language describing psychological phenomena from language describing non-psychological phenomena. His criteria for intentional language include independence from existence, indifference to truth-value, and referential opacity. In contemporary discussions within artificial intelligence and the philosophy of mind, intentionality remains a contentious topic. Some argue that machines will never achieve intentionality. John Searle, for instance, supported this view with his Chinese Room thought experiment, asserting that syntactic operations in computers cannot produce semantic content. However, Searle's position is a minority view in these fields. Daniel Dennett, in his book The Intentional Stance, provides a taxonomy of current theories of intentionality. Most modern theories accept Brentano's thesis of the irreducibility of intentional idioms. From this thesis, two positions emerge: (1) that intentional idioms are problematic for science, and (2) that they are not problematic for science. Advocates of the first position, such as Chisholm, Anscombe, Geach, and Taylor, argue that intentional idioms cannot be integrated with natural sciences and often maintain realism regarding intentional objects, which may imply a form of dualism. In contrast, realists like Jerry Fodor, Burge, Dretske, Kripke, and the early Hilary Putnam argue for a deeper ontological reality to translation and belief attribution, grounding intentionality in a language of thought. Dennett critiques this approach, suggesting that such irreducible realities are made acceptable to physical sciences by linking them to the syntax of physically realized mental representations. Dennett also introduces the concept of the intentional stance, a predictive strategy that attributes beliefs to physical systems if doing so successfully predicts their behavior. This position is further divided into two principles: the Normative Principle and the Projective Principle. Advocates of the Normative Principle argue that attributions of intentional idioms should reflect the propositional attitudes a system ought to have in given circumstances. This view is further split between those who assume rationality and those who adhere to the Principle of Charity. Proponents of the Assumption of Rationality, such as Dennett, Cherniak, and the later Putnam, assume that the system in question is rational. Meanwhile, Donald Davidson and Lewis defend the Principle of Charity. It is important to note that intentionality should not be confused with intensionality, a concept from semantics, although the two are related in the context of modern understandings of intention.
